title: Improving Intrusion Detection for Imbalanced Network Traffic using Generative Deep Learning
summary: Treats intrusion detection as a class-imbalance problem first and a classification problem second, oversampling the attack classes of standard IDS benchmarks before fitting SVM, decision tree and neural classifiers, and separately scoring the quality of the generated records rather than only the downstream detection rate. CTGAN is the paper's method rather than one of its comparisons: it is run as the oversampler for every configuration, and the stated contributions are applying CTGAN to intrusion-detection imbalance and evaluating the data it generates.
evidence: the abstract states that the authors employed a conditional tabular generative adversarial network (CTGAN) model with common machine learning algorithms to build more effective detection systems while addressing the imbalance issue, and that CTGAN can generate samples of the minority class during training to make the dataset more balanced, combined with support vector machine and two further learners; the introduction states the focus of the study is on oversampling techniques, specifically an enhanced version of GAN, the conditional tabular GAN, describing it as a recent deep learning model that can be thought of as an oversampling technique able to augment a tabular dataset and increase the frequency of minority class samples; the stated contributions are handling the imbalance problem in intrusion detection datasets by employing CTGAN, which is not investigated very well in the literature, and evaluating the quality of the data CTGAN generates; the background reproduces CTGAN's conditional generator formulation and credits it with combining the advantages of CGAN and TGAN, controlling class labels of generated samples and overcoming non-Gaussian and multimodal distributions using fully connected networks

title: Ensemble feature selection and tabular data augmentation with generative adversarial networks to enhance cutaneous melanoma identification and interpretability
summary: Combines ensemble feature selection with tabular augmentation to identify melanoma from dermoscopy-derived features on two small, imbalanced public datasets, then uses SHAP, bootstrap tests and UMAP to make the resulting models interpretable to clinicians. CTGAN is the augmenter throughout: it synthesizes rows in the extracted feature and embedding space at controlled imbalance ratios, and the paper's best reported results are the combination of ensemble feature selection, CTGAN and linear models.
evidence: the abstract states the authors propose to combine ensemble feature selection methods and data augmentation with conditional tabular generative adversarial networks (CTGAN) to enhance melanoma identification in imbalanced datasets, and reports that the combination of ensemble FS, CTGAN and linear models achieved the best predictive results, with AUCROC of 87 per cent on PH2 and 76 per cent on Derm7pt; the background states that the novel conditional tabular GAN has shown excellent performance in addressing the main issues in generating mixed-type tabular data and that it handles categorical and continuous variables because it uses mode-specific normalization, adding that CTGAN has been benchmarked against other generative models with high performance; the methods state that data augmentation was performed using CTGAN on image features and image embeddings extracted from the Derm7pt and PH2 skin datasets, with the volume of aggregated synthetic samples controlled by the imbalance ratio

title: Conditional Generative Model Based Predicate-Aware Query Approximation
summary: Proposes ELECTRA, an approximate query processing method that learns a conditional generative model over a database so that a query with several predicates can be answered from generated samples rather than from a stored uniform sample, which is where sampling-based AQP loses accuracy on selective queries. CTGAN is one of the generative baselines run for comparison, taken from the sdv-dev repository, and the paper's motivating limitation is CTGAN's support for only a single generation condition, which forces the authors to pick one predicate at random when using it.
evidence: the evaluation states that CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019) is a conditional generative model, but that the CTGAN technique as described in the paper and the associated code support at most one condition for generation, so when using CTGAN as a baseline the authors randomly select one of the input predicates as the condition for generating samples; the reference list cites CTGAN code, 2019, CTGAN Github Repo, https://github.com/sdv-dev/CTGAN, accessed 2022-04-29, which identifies the implementation run; the results report the distribution of AQP errors over the queries each technique could support, noting cases where ELECTRA, CTGAN and VAE-AQP could not match the used predicates in the generated data, and state that as the number of predicates increases the approximation error is almost always lowest for ELECTRA while the other two generative baselines, CTGAN and VAE-AQP, perform poorly; ELECTRA's own conditioning mechanism is its own contribution rather than an adoption of CTGAN's conditional vector

title: A Learnable Discrete-Prior Fusion Autoencoder with Contrastive Learning for Tabular Data Synthesis
summary: Proposes GTCoder, an autoencoder for tabular synthesis that learns a discrete prior and fuses it with a continuous one, trained with a contrastive objective so that the latent space separates the discrete and continuous modes that mixed-type tables carry. CTGAN and TVAE are two of the six deep baselines it is measured against, appearing as rows in both the machine-learning utility tables across six datasets and the likelihood tables on the synthetic grid and ring distributions.
evidence: the introduction groups the prior synthesis methods as Bayesian-network based, GAN-based (Xu et al. 2019 among them) and VAE-based (Xu et al. 2019 again, for TVAE); the related-work section states that CTGAN is proposed in Xu et al. 2019 for tabular data synthesis and has been shown to be better than Bayesian networks; the comparison-methods section states that for synthetic data quality the authors compare GTCoder with three GAN-based methods, CTGAN, bi-discriminator GAN and WGAN, and three VAE-based methods, TVAE, LVAE and GMVAE, training all methods with the same epoch count and batch size for fairness; the utility table reports macro and weighted F1 for CTGAN and TVAE against GTCoder across Sonar, News and four further datasets, and the likelihood table reports Lsyn and Ltest for both on grid, gridr and ring

title: Quality-Aware Self-Training on Differentiable Synthesis of Rare Relational Data
summary: Proposes QAST, which synthesizes rare-class relational records and then judges its own output, attaching semantic pseudo-labels to generated samples and filtering them by a learned quality estimate so that self-training does not amplify bad synthetic data, addressing the fact that GAN samples arrive without reliable labels. CTGAN is both a compared baseline in the distribution figures and the design QAST's own generator follows: the shared GAN module's generator and the normalization of the original samples are taken from Xu et al.
evidence: Figure 1 compares the projected feature distributions of the proposed QAST method against two comparative baselines, CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019) and GLGAN, alongside the original data; the related-work section states that the Conditional Tabular GAN exploits a conditional generator to generate relational data, and that although tricks such as mode-specific normalization and a conditional generator can be applied, GAN samples typically lack semantic labels, which is the gap QAST addresses; the method states that the shared GAN module consists of a generator following Xu et al. 2019 to generate samples approaching the real distribution, and the reconstruction loss is defined over X, the set of the normalized original samples by following Xu et al. 2019. Importance 4 under the MTGAN precedent: the paper both benchmarks CTGAN and builds its own generator and normalization on CTGAN's design

title: Improving robustness and explainability of PE malware classifiers using GAN-Generated Synthetic Adversarial examples
summary: Proposes an adversarial training scheme for Windows PE malware classifiers that avoids the cost of crafting functionality-preserving malicious binaries: real adversarial files are mapped into a tabular feature space, that distribution is then expanded synthetically, and classifiers trained on the expansion are tested against five realistic PE attacks under leakage-safe cross-validation. CTGAN produces those synthetic adversarial examples, so the defence the paper proposes is CTGAN output applied to each attack-specific distribution.
evidence: the abstract states the authors propose a novel defense methodology that augments unrealistic synthetic adversarial examples into standard adversarial training, produced using the Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN), and evaluates random forest, LightGBM and MLP classifiers against five realistic Windows PE attacks including Full DOS and EXTEND; the related-work comparison states that the proposed approach synthetically expands the adversarial distribution in the training set through CTGAN-generated examples, eliminating the need to craft new realistic adversarial files; the method walkthrough states that the authors map clean and adversarial binaries into a tabular feature space and then expand each attack-specific adversarial distribution using CTGAN-synthesized features before training and evaluating under leakage-safe cross-validation, citing Xu et al. (2019)

title: Browser Fingerprinting: How to Protect Machine Learning Models and Data with Differential Privacy?
summary: Shows that a browser can be identified from network traffic features alone, then asks what it costs to defend the resulting model and its training data with differential privacy, comparing DP-SGD on the classifier against releasing a differentially private synthetic dataset instead. The synthetic-data arm runs PATE-CTGAN together with QUAIL: PATE-CTGAN is Rosenblatt et al.'s CTGAN variant that trains the generator under the PATE framework, so the paper's privacy-preserving dataset is produced by a named third-party CTGAN descendant.
evidence: the contributions state that the authors evaluate the utility of differentially private synthetic data by applying machine learning algorithms to it, and that in this case data is protected directly with QUAIL and PATE-CTGAN by creating a synthetic dataset that guarantees differential privacy, citing Rosenblatt et al.; the related-work section states that Rosenblatt et al. build upon Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN) (Xu et al. 2019), applying the PATE framework to CTGAN to create PATE-CTGAN and separately adding noise to the discriminator to produce DP-CTGAN, and that the same authors propose QUAIL; the method section states that to protect the raw dataset the authors create a differentially private synthetic dataset for browser fingerprinting by applying PATE-CTGAN and QUAIL, describing PATE-CTGAN as based on the PATE framework and PATE-GAN
needs: Same convention gap as paper-nft-data-trading-dpctgan-2025 (shard 55): a named third-party CTGAN derivative is run as the production generator rather than benchmarked. Recorded api_user 4 to match that precedent; `inherited` 3 is the alternative. This is now the second instance, so the ruling settles a recurring pattern rather than a one-off

title: TextBrew: Automated Model Selection and Hyperparameter Optimization for Text Classification
summary: Builds an AutoML system for text classification that predicts which model family will win on a new dataset from cheap meta-features, then tunes and ensembles the winners, sidestepping the cost of trying every transformer. The meta-model's training data is the bottleneck, because public text-classification datasets are scarce, and CopulaGAN fills it: the SDV synthesizer generates 150 meta-dataset rows per candidate-model group, keeping the meta-dataset balanced.
evidence: the abstract states that because text classification datasets are not abundant the system generates synthetic data to augment the meta-dataset using CopulaGAN, a deep generative model, and CopulaGAN is listed among the paper's keywords; the pipeline description states that due to the small size of the meta-dataset on which the meta-model is trained, CopulaGAN is used to synthesize additional data to help the meta-model train better; the synthesis section states the authors employ the CopulaGAN model to generate 150 data points for each group of datasets having a particular candidate model as the best, ensuring the resulting dataset is not unbalanced, and states that the CopulaGAN model is a variation of the CTGAN model which takes advantage of the CDF-based transformation that the GaussianCopulas apply to make the underlying CTGAN model's task of learning the data easier

title: Computational analysis of the Logistics Supply Chain from a global trade perspective
summary: Ranks five logistics supply chain factors for global trade using fuzzy AHP with triangular fuzzy numbers and a PROMETHEE-style outranking step, driven by pairwise judgements elicited from industry practitioners and researchers, and concludes that promoting export dominates the alternatives. SDV enters only as a cited name: both the Patki thesis and the Patki, Wedge and Veeramachaneni paper sit in the bibliography and the phrase augmenting synthetic data vault appears in the method, but no synthesizer is run and no synthetic data is characterised anywhere in the paper.
evidence: the method section states that the development assessment of the logistics supply chain employs data and experts' opinions, that AHP based on insight from industrialists, professionals and researchers is used to establish priority selection, and that moreover the data is backed by an augmenting synthetic data vault, citing Schoenherr (2009) and Althaqafi (2020), neither of which is an SDV work; the conclusion repeats that the factor ranking is on the basis of expert opinion and synthetic data vault; the bibliography carries both Patki's MIT thesis, The synthetic data vault: generative modeling for relational databases, and Patki, Wedge and Veeramachaneni, The Synthetic Data Vault, DSAA 2016. No SDV component, synthesizer, metric or synthetic dataset is described anywhere in the body, and the inline Patki citations are attached instead to claims about logistics and supply-chain terminology that neither SDV work contains
needs: The SDV citations in this paper appear misapplied rather than substantive: Patki (2016) is cited inline for definitional claims about logistics and supply chain management, and the one methodological mention of the synthetic data vault carries citations to two unrelated works. Recorded citation_only importance 1 on the ground that the SDV papers are genuinely in the bibliography. Saman may prefer to drop the entry entirely, as three papers were dropped from the IEEE lane for having no real SDV content

title: CTAB-GAN+: enhancing tabular data synthesis
summary: Extends CTAB-GAN into CTAB-GAN+, adding a feature encoder for single-Gaussian variables, a Wasserstein-plus-gradient-penalty loss with a downstream-task loss, a redesigned conditional vector for imbalanced categorical and continuous variables, and DP-SGD training, then evaluates against nine tabular generators on seven datasets both with and without a privacy budget. CTGAN is the substrate this lineage descends from and a benchmarked baseline at once: CTAB-GAN+ adopts Xu et al.'s mode-specific normalization directly, builds its conditional vector on CTGAN's, and reports CTGAN and TVAE rows throughout.
evidence: the design section states that to handle the complex distributions of continuous columns the authors adopted the Mode-Specific Normalization (MSN) method (Xu et al., 2019), encoding each value as a value-mode pair based on a variational Gaussian mixture model, and that CTAB-GAN+ incorporates Was+GP, downstream, information and generator losses citing Xu et al. 2019 among the sources, with a newly designed conditional vector to counter mode collapse for imbalanced categorical and continuous variables; the related-work section states that CTGAN and TVAE (both Xu et al., 2019) used a variational Gaussian mixture to encode continuous columns and that CTGAN also adopts training-by-sampling, which leverages the conditional vector; the evaluation states CTAB-GAN+ is tested on seven datasets against nine algorithms including CTGAN and TVAE, outperforming all baselines by at least 33.5 per cent on accuracy, and the distribution analysis discusses where CTGAN's variational Gaussian mixture loses modes. The paper extends CTAB-GAN (Zhao et al., 2021), itself a CTGAN derivative, so this is a second-generation named variant that still adopts CTGAN's own encoder and conditional-vector design
